description: We are five enthusiastic students from Shivamogga, Karnataka, participating in NASA’s space program. We are interested in space science, technology, coding, design, and solving real-world challenges. Our team values creativity, teamwork, and learning. We are looking for one more member skilled in programming, data analysis, design, electronics, research, or presentation. Join us if you enjoy innovative ideas and collaborative problem-solving.”
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web app that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare candidate landing sites at the Moon’s south pole and find when each site has both sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth. We combine NASA LOLA 80 m elevation data with hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons for all of 2027. For each site, we compute the terrain skyline in 360 directions and check hour by hour whether the Sun and Earth are above it. The app shows an answer card with the best site and best 7-day window, a south-pole map, a sky view of the Sun and Earth against the terrain horizon, a year-long timeline, and an explainable comparison with adjustable weights and plain-language reasons. In our results, Site C is the best geometric opportunity, with a 168-hour window from 13 to 20 January 2027 in which both are visible throughout. This matters because the Sun and Earth stay near the horizon at the pole, so terrain decides power and communication. The results are geometric visibility only. Slope and roughness safety are not yet assessed. The code is open on GitHub.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners, educators and the public answer two questions at the Moon’s south pole: where to land and when. For each candidate site it shows when the Sun (for power) and Earth (for direct communication) are above the local terrain skyline, hour by hour across 2027.

How it works

  1. We read real lunar terrain heights from the NASA LOLA 80 m elevation map.
  2. For each site we compute the terrain skyline in all 360 compass directions (observer height 2 m).
  3. We pull hourly Sun and Earth positions for 2027 (8,761 hours) from NASA/JPL Horizons.
  4. A body counts as visible when its elevation plus its apparent radius (Sun 0.27°, Earth 0.95°) is above the skyline.
  5. We score the sites (default 70% Sun, 30% Earth, adjustable in the app) and explain the ranking in plain language using the actual numbers.

What the app shows

  • An answer card with the best site and the best 7-day window
  • A south-pole map of the candidate sites
  • A sky view of the Sun and Earth against the terrain horizon
  • A year-long visibility timeline
  • A comparison table with sliders and A-versus-B explanations

Results

Site C ranks first: the Sun is visible 50.2% of 2027 and Earth 100%. Its best 7-day window runs from 13 to 20 January 2027, with both visible throughout. We cross-checked our Sun values against NASA’s long-term visibility maps, and they agree within about 3 percentage points.

Impact and benefits

NASA’s visibility maps show long-term averages. Our tool shows when, and it accounts for terrain, so it makes site and date comparison fast and easy to understand for non-experts. The app is explainable, runs offline from precomputed data, and the code is open on GitHub.

Tools used

NASA LOLA data (PGDA), NASA/JPL Horizons API, Python for the data pipeline, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Recharts for the web app, Vercel for hosting, GitHub, and AI assistants (Claude and Antigravity) for coding and documentation.

Creativity

We combine terrain-aware visibility, hourly ephemeris data and an explainable score on one page, with a sky view that shows exactly why a site is blocked.

Factors we considered and limitations

We considered terrain blocking, Earth and Sun apparent size, observer height and mission length. Results are geometric visibility only, not a radio-link or solar-power model. Slope and roughness safety are not yet assessed. The analysis covers 2027 on an 80 m terrain grid with hourly steps. Site A shows no Earth visibility in 2027, which differs from NASA’s long-term map and which we are still reviewing.

Next steps

Add slope, roughness and shadowed-region safety from 20 m data, add solar-power and radio-link models, screen more candidate sites automatically, and extend to many years of data.
